## Why SDF

Source: https://stacked-diffs-flow.com/docs/why-sdf/

What stacked diffs solve, how SDF compares to alternatives, and whether it's the right fit for your team.

# Why SDF

## The problem: large PRs

Most teams develop features that span multiple files, layers, or concerns. The natural instinct is to work on a single branch and open one pull request when the feature is ready. But large PRs create problems:

- **Reviews take longer and are less thorough.** A 2,000-line PR overwhelms reviewers. They skim instead of reading carefully, and bugs slip through.
- **Feedback arrives late.** If a reviewer questions a design decision made in the first 200 lines, the remaining 1,800 lines may need to be reworked.
- **CI takes longer.** Large diffs increase test flakiness and make failures harder to diagnose.
- **Merging is risky.** The bigger the diff, the higher the chance of a conflict with other work happening in parallel.

The solution is to break work into a chain of small, dependent PRs &mdash; each one building on the last, each one reviewable on its own. This is the stacked diffs workflow.

## What stacked diffs give you

A stack is a linear chain of branches where each branch is based on the one before it:

```
main ← db-schema ← repository ← controller
         PR #1        PR #2        PR #3
```

Each PR shows only its own diff &mdash; not the accumulated diff of every layer below it. Reviewers see focused changes. Authors get feedback early on foundational decisions. PRs can be approved and merged independently, from the bottom up.

The catch is that stacking requires rebasing. When the bottom PR is updated or merged, every branch above it must be rebased and force-pushed. The PR bases on GitHub must be updated. This is tedious and error-prone by hand &mdash; which is why tools like SDF exist.

The benefits are well-proven at scale. Major engineering organizations have adopted stacked diffs as a core workflow and built dedicated tooling around it &mdash; Meta open-sourced [Sapling](https://sapling-scm.com), a full source control system with native stacking support, and Google's internal code review system has long been built around small, dependent changes. The pattern works; the challenge has been making it accessible outside these environments.

## What SDF does

SDF is a CLI tool that manages the full lifecycle of stacked PRs on GitHub:

- **Creates stacks** with `sdf new` and adds branches with `sdf branch`
- **Creates PRs** with `sdf pr`, automatically setting the correct base branch and adding stack navigation links to each PR description
- **Syncs after merges** with `sdf sync` &mdash; detects merged PRs, cascade-rebases all downstream branches, force-pushes, and updates PR bases on GitHub
- **Resolves conflicts with AI** &mdash; when a rebase conflict occurs during sync, Claude receives the full context (upstream changes, PR description, conflicted files) and resolves the conflict in place
- **Splits large branches** with `sdf split` &mdash; Claude analyzes a branch and decomposes it into a stack of focused PRs

## How SDF compares to alternatives

### vs. Graphite

[Graphite](https://graphite.dev) is a commercial SaaS platform with a CLI, a VS Code extension, a web-based PR inbox, a merge queue, AI code review, and engineering metrics. It is the most fully-featured option in this space.

**Where Graphite shines:** Graphite is a platform, not just a CLI. Its web UI provides a purpose-built PR inbox, merge queue, CI skip for intermediate PRs, and engineering analytics. If your team wants an integrated experience that replaces parts of the GitHub UI, Graphite delivers that. The CLI is polished with excellent tab completion and a well-documented command set.

**Where SDF differs:** SDF stores state locally &mdash; no cloud dependency, no account, no vendor approval. An individual engineer can `brew install` it and start stacking today without a team-wide mandate. SDF's AI-powered conflict resolution during rebases is unique &mdash; when a cascade rebase hits a conflict, Claude resolves it in-place using the PR description and upstream diff as context. SDF also provides `sdf split` for AI-powered decomposition of large branches into stacks. Graphite requires the team to operate within its ecosystem; SDF works alongside your existing GitHub workflow without replacing any part of it.

### vs. ghstack

[ghstack](https://github.com/ezyang/ghstack) is an open-source Python CLI widely used in the PyTorch/Meta ecosystem. It treats each commit as a PR &mdash; one commit, one PR, no separate branches in your working tree.

**Where ghstack shines:** ghstack's commit-centric model is elegant for its use case: you work on a single branch, each commit becomes a separate PR, and `ghstack push` syncs everything. There's no branch management overhead &mdash; your working tree stays simple. The mental model is straightforward once internalized, and it has a strong track record in large-scale open source projects.

**Where SDF differs:** SDF is branch-centric &mdash; each PR lives on its own branch. This means you can work on any layer independently (add commits, run tests, iterate on review feedback) without affecting other PRs in the stack. SDF doesn't constrain how you merge: click "Squash and merge" in the GitHub UI, use `gh pr merge` from the terminal, or run `sdf merge` &mdash; it all works. The next `sdf sync` detects what happened on GitHub and reconciles automatically. ghstack PRs require `ghstack land` or a custom GitHub Action to merge, which means reviewers and CI bots need to know about the tool. SDF also provides AI conflict resolution, PR content generation, and `sdf split` for decomposing branches &mdash; features ghstack doesn't offer.

### vs. git town

[git town](https://git-town.com) is a mature open-source Go CLI that provides high-level Git workflow commands. It supports stacking as one of many workflow modes and works with GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, and Gitea.

**Where git town shines:** git town supports multiple Git hosting platforms (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Gitea) and is a general-purpose workflow tool, not just a stacking tool. It has a large community, extensive documentation, and covers a wide range of Git workflows beyond stacking (feature branches, contribution, ship/sync patterns). If your team uses something other than GitHub or wants one tool for multiple workflow styles, git town is the more versatile choice.

**Where SDF differs:** SDF is stacking-first &mdash; every feature is designed specifically for the stacked PRs workflow. It provides PR creation with automatic base targeting and stack navigation links, AI-assisted conflict resolution during cascade rebases, and AI-powered branch splitting. These are purpose-built for stacking and not available in git town.

### vs. spr

[spr](https://github.com/ejoffe/spr) is an open-source Go CLI with a similar philosophy to ghstack &mdash; each commit is an atomic PR. Run `git spr update` and it syncs your commit stack to GitHub as individual PRs.

**Where spr shines:** spr has the simplest interface of any stacking tool: one command (`git spr update`) syncs your entire stack. Like ghstack, the commit-centric model keeps your working tree clean &mdash; one branch, one stack. It integrates as a git subcommand, which feels native. The tool is lightweight and focused.

**Where SDF differs:** SDF's branch-centric model provides more flexibility &mdash; you can work on branches independently, add multiple commits per PR, and switch between layers freely. SDF handles the full PR lifecycle (creation, base updates, navigation links, content generation) rather than just syncing state. The AI features (conflict resolution, branch splitting, PR descriptions) address the pain points that make stacking hard at scale.

### vs. Sapling

[Sapling](https://sapling-scm.com) is a full source control system from Meta with native stacking support. It can interact with Git repositories and GitHub but is fundamentally a different SCM.

**Where Sapling shines:** Sapling has first-class stacking built into the SCM itself &mdash; not bolted on as a separate tool. Its `sl` commands, smartlog visualization, and commit-centric model are refined by years of use at Meta scale. If you're willing to adopt a new SCM, it offers the deepest stacking integration of any tool in this list. It also supports non-linear stack topologies that SDF doesn't.

**Where SDF differs:** SDF works with the Git and GitHub workflow your team already uses &mdash; no new SCM to learn, no migration, no tooling changes for CI or code review. The adoption cost is minimal: install a single binary and keep using `git`, `gh`, and GitHub as before. SDF also provides AI features (conflict resolution, branch splitting) that Sapling doesn't have.

### vs. manual `git rebase --update-refs`

Git 2.38 added `--update-refs` to `git rebase`, which automatically updates stacked branch refs during a rebase.

**Where `--update-refs` shines:** It's built into Git &mdash; zero dependencies, zero installation. For engineers who are comfortable with rebase mechanics and only need occasional stacking, it eliminates the most tedious part (updating sibling branch pointers) without adding any tooling.

**Where SDF differs:** `--update-refs` handles local branch ref updates but leaves everything else manual. Here's what a typical sync looks like with `--update-refs` vs. SDF after the bottom PR in a 3-branch stack merges:

With `--update-refs`:

```bash
git fetch origin
git checkout main && git pull
git rebase --update-refs main branch-3
# resolve any conflicts manually...
git push --force-with-lease origin branch-2
git push --force-with-lease origin branch-3
gh pr edit 201 --base main           # fix PR base (otherwise diff shows all of main)
gh pr edit 202 --base branch-2       # fix next PR base too
# manually update PR descriptions if you maintain stack navigation links
```

With SDF:

```bash
sdf sync
```

That single command detects the merge, cascade-rebases both branches, force-pushes them, updates PR bases on GitHub, and refreshes the stack navigation links in every PR description. If a conflict occurs, Claude resolves it using the PR description and upstream diff as context. The manual workflow works, but it scales linearly with the number of branches &mdash; and forgetting the `gh pr edit --base` step leaves GitHub showing broken diffs until you notice.

## When to use SDF

SDF is a good fit when:

- You develop on **GitHub** and want to use stacked PRs
- You prefer **branch-centric** workflows (one branch per PR)
- You want a tool that works **alongside** your existing workflow, not a platform that replaces it
- You value **local-first** tooling &mdash; no accounts, no servers, no vendor dependencies
- You already use **AI tools** in your development workflow and want that to extend to branch management, conflict resolution, and PR authoring

## When NOT to use SDF

SDF is not the right choice when:

- You use **GitLab, Bitbucket, or another non-GitHub host** &mdash; SDF is GitHub-only
- You prefer **commit-centric** stacking (one commit = one PR) &mdash; use ghstack or spr instead
- You need a **platform** with merge queues, analytics, and a web inbox &mdash; use Graphite
- You need **non-linear** dependency graphs &mdash; SDF supports only linear stacks

## Maturity and status

SDF is in active development (v0.3.x). The command surface is stable and the tool is used in production by its author and early adopters. It is MIT-licensed, open-source, and has no server-side component.

The Claude CLI dependency is **optional**. Without it, SDF falls back to manual conflict resolution and generates PR titles from branch names and commit subjects. Branch splitting (`sdf split`) requires the Claude CLI.

**Install:** `brew install pavelpascari/tap/sdf`
**Repository:** [github.com/pavelpascari/sdf](https://github.com/pavelpascari/sdf)
**License:** MIT

## Getting Started

Source: https://stacked-diffs-flow.com/docs/getting-started/

Build and sync your first stacked PR chain in under five minutes.

# Getting Started

SDF turns the painful work of managing stacked pull requests into a single command. This guide walks you through creating your first stack, adding layers, and syncing after a PR merges.

## Prerequisites

- **git** &mdash; any recent version
- **gh** (GitHub CLI) &mdash; authenticated with `gh auth login`
- **sdf** &mdash; see [Installation](/docs/installation)

Run the health check first:

```bash
sdf doctor
```

All green? Set up your environment:

```bash
# Shell completions -- tab-complete commands, flags, branches, and stacks
sdf completion install

# Teach Claude Code how to use SDF (optional, requires Claude CLI)
sdf ai intro
```

`sdf completion install` auto-detects your shell and writes the completion script to the right location. `sdf ai intro` creates a [skill file](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/claude-code/skills) so Claude remembers SDF commands and workflows across sessions.

---

## 1. Create a stack

A *stack* is a named chain of branches. Each branch becomes a PR that depends on the one above it.

```bash
# Creates the stack and checks out the first branch in one step
sdf new --branch db-schema users-feature
```

This creates:

- A stack named `users-feature` with `main` as the base
- A branch `users-feature/db-schema` checked out and ready (prefixed with the stack name by default)
- `.sdf/stacks/users-feature.json` to track topology

Output:

```
Initialized stack "users-feature" (base: main)
Created branch "users-feature/db-schema" (based on main)

Next steps:
  sdf pr               Create a pull request
  sdf branch <name>    Add another branch to the stack
  sdf status           View stack topology
```

## 2. Write code and create the PR

Do your work on the branch, commit as usual, then create a pull request:

```bash
# ... implement schema migration ...
git add -A && git commit -m "add users table migration"

sdf pr
```

This pushes the branch and runs `gh pr create` with a body that identifies the stack:

```
Part of stack: **users-feature**

Base: `main`
```

SDF also updates all PR descriptions in the stack with navigation links so reviewers can jump between related PRs.

## 3. Add more layers

```bash
sdf branch repository
# ... implement UserRepository ...
sdf pr

sdf branch controller
# ... implement endpoints ...
sdf pr
```

Each `sdf branch` creates a new branch prefixed with the stack name (e.g. `users-feature/repository`, `users-feature/controller`) and positions it after your current branch in the stack.

Check the stack at any time:

```bash
sdf status
```

```
  users-feature  (base: main)

 → ● users-feature/db-schema      PR #142  open      in sync
   ● users-feature/repository     PR #143  open      in sync
   ● users-feature/controller     PR #144  open      in sync
```

The `→` marker shows which branch you currently have checked out. Each line shows the branch name, PR number, status, and sync state.

## 4. Sync after a merge

When PR #142 (db-schema) is approved and merged:

```bash
sdf sync
```

SDF will:

1. Fetch from origin and fast-forward the base branch
2. Query GitHub for merged PRs and update their status in the stack
3. Rebase each downstream branch onto its new parent (skipping merged nodes)
4. Push updated branches with `git push --force-with-lease`
5. Update PR base branches on GitHub so diffs render correctly

If conflicts occur, SDF presents an interactive menu:

- **Ask Claude to resolve** (if Claude CLI is installed) &mdash; Claude reads the upstream changes and the PR description to attempt automatic resolution
- **Fix it yourself** &mdash; pauses the sync so you can resolve manually, then resume with `sdf sync --continue`
- **Skip this branch** &mdash; aborts the rebase for that branch and continues with the rest
- **Abort sync** &mdash; stops everything

Merged nodes stay in the stack as completed entries rather than being removed, so you can see the full history with `sdf status`.

---

## Alternative: split an existing branch

Already have a large branch you want to break into reviewable pieces? `sdf split` uses Claude to decompose it into a stack automatically:

```bash
sdf split --from feature/big-change --stack my-feature
```

Claude analyzes the diff, identifies semantic themes, and proposes a split plan. After your review, SDF creates the branches, validates the split is lossless, pushes, and creates PRs. The original branch is never modified.

See [AI Features](/docs/ai-features) for details on how the analysis works, and the [Commands reference](/docs/commands) for all `sdf split` flags.

---

## What Are Stacked Diffs?

Source: https://stacked-diffs-flow.com/docs/what-are-stacked-diffs/

A practical explanation of stacked pull requests, why teams use them, and how SDF automates the maintenance work.

# What Are Stacked Diffs?

Stacked diffs (also called stacked pull requests) are a way to split one large feature into a sequence of smaller PRs that depend on each other.

Instead of opening one 2,000-line PR, you open a stack like this:

```text
main <- db-schema <- repository <- controller
         PR #1        PR #2         PR #3
```

Each PR stays focused on one concern. Reviewers can approve bottom-up, and feedback arrives earlier.

## Why engineers use stacked pull requests

- **Smaller reviews**: focused PRs are easier to read and discuss.
- **Faster iteration**: design feedback lands before the entire feature is complete.
- **Lower merge risk**: smaller diffs reduce surprise conflicts.
- **Parallel progress**: you can keep working on upper layers while lower PRs are under review.

## Why stacked diffs are hard without tooling

When PR #1 changes or merges, every downstream branch must be rebased and force-pushed. Then PR base branches on GitHub often need retargeting.

Manual workflow usually means:

1. Rebase branch 2 onto updated `main`
2. Rebase branch 3 onto updated branch 2
3. Push both with `--force-with-lease`
4. Update PR base targets and navigation links

That maintenance work grows linearly with stack size.

## How SDF helps

SDF automates the painful parts:

- `sdf new` and `sdf branch` create and extend stacks
- `sdf pr` opens PRs with correct base targets
- `sdf sync` detects merges, cascade-rebases downstream branches, and updates PR bases
- `sdf split` decomposes a large branch into a reviewable stack

If you want the full conceptual model, continue with [Core Concepts](/docs/core-concepts). If you want to start right away, use [Getting Started](/docs/getting-started).

---

## Installation

Source: https://stacked-diffs-flow.com/docs/installation/

Install SDF on macOS, Linux, or Windows.

# Installation

SDF ships as a single static binary. Pick the method that fits your workflow.

---

## Homebrew (macOS and Linux)

```bash
brew install pavelpascari/tap/sdf
```

Updates are handled by `brew upgrade`.

---

## Go install

If you have Go 1.24 or later:

```bash
go install github.com/pavelpascari/sdf@latest
```

The binary is placed in `$GOPATH/bin` (ensure this is on your `$PATH`).

---

## Binary download

Pre-built binaries are available for every platform on the [Releases page](https://github.com/pavelpascari/sdf/releases).

| Platform | Architecture | File |
|---|---|---|
| Linux | x86_64 | `sdf-linux-amd64.tar.gz` |
| Linux | ARM64 | `sdf-linux-arm64.tar.gz` |
| macOS | Intel | `sdf-darwin-amd64.tar.gz` |
| macOS | Apple Silicon | `sdf-darwin-arm64.tar.gz` |
| Windows | x86_64 | `sdf-windows-amd64.zip` |
| Windows | ARM64 | `sdf-windows-arm64.zip` |

GoReleaser produces a single `checksums.txt` file covering all archives. Verify before running:

```bash
# Download and verify (Linux x86_64 example)
curl -LO https://github.com/pavelpascari/sdf/releases/latest/download/sdf-linux-amd64.tar.gz
curl -LO https://github.com/pavelpascari/sdf/releases/latest/download/checksums.txt
sha256sum -c --ignore-missing checksums.txt
tar xzf sdf-linux-amd64.tar.gz
mv sdf /usr/local/bin/
```

---

## Build from source

```bash
git clone https://github.com/pavelpascari/sdf.git
cd sdf
make build      # → bin/sdf
make install    # → $GOPATH/bin/sdf
```

Requires Go 1.24+.

---

## Runtime dependencies

SDF shells out to other CLIs rather than reimplementing their logic:

| Dependency | Required for | Install |
|---|---|---|
| `git` | All operations | Comes with your OS |
| `gh` | PR operations (`sdf pr`, `sdf sync`) | [cli.github.com](https://cli.github.com) |
| `claude` | AI features | [claude.ai/code](https://claude.ai/code) |

The Claude CLI is optional. Without it, `sdf sync` will open `$EDITOR` on conflicts instead of resolving them automatically.

Verify everything is in place:

```bash
sdf doctor
```

---

## Uninstall

Remove the binary from wherever you placed it. SDF writes no data outside the repositories you use it in (plus `~/.config/sdf/config.json` for global config).

```bash
# If installed via Homebrew
brew uninstall sdf

# If installed manually
rm $(which sdf)
rm -rf ~/.config/sdf
```

---

## Core Concepts

Source: https://stacked-diffs-flow.com/docs/core-concepts/

Stacks, nodes, and how SDF models your PR chains.

# Core Concepts

## Design principles

SDF is built around three principles:

**Shell out, don't reimplement.** SDF delegates to `git`, `gh`, and `claude` CLIs. It is pure orchestration &mdash; no custom git library, no custom GitHub API client. This means you get the behavior of the tools you already know and trust.

**PR descriptions are the source of truth.** Since `.sdf/` is local-only, the authoritative record of stack structure and intent lives in the PR descriptions on GitHub. SDF can reconstruct stack topology from the PR graph via `sdf fetch`, making the workflow resilient to lost local state.

**Fail loudly, recover clearly.** When something goes wrong, SDF leaves the repository in a known state and tells you exactly what to run to recover. It never silently swallows errors.

---

Understanding SDF's model makes every command feel obvious. There are two things to know: **stacks** and **nodes**.

---

## Stacks

A *stack* is a named, linear chain of branches that all descend from a common base (usually `main`). Each branch in the chain becomes a pull request that depends on the PR above it.

```
main
 └─ users-feature/db-schema      ← PR #142
     └─ users-feature/repository  ← PR #143
         └─ users-feature/controller ← PR #144
```

A repository can have **multiple independent stacks** &mdash; one for each feature being developed in parallel. Each stack has its own JSON file in `.sdf/stacks/<name>.json`, stored locally on your machine.

### Stack JSON

```json
{
  "stack_id": "users-feature",
  "base": "main",
  "nodes": [
    { "branch": "users-feature/db-schema",   "pr": 142, "status": "open",   "base_tip": "abc123", "nav_hash": "e3b0c4..." },
    { "branch": "users-feature/repository",  "pr": 143, "status": "open",   "base_tip": "def456" },
    { "branch": "users-feature/controller",  "pr": 144, "status": "draft",  "base_tip": "ghi789" }
  ]
}
```

The `base_tip` records the commit hash at the tip of the parent branch at the time of the last sync. This allows SDF to detect when a parent has moved and a rebase is needed.

The optional `nav_hash` is a SHA-256 hash of the PR stack navigation section. SDF uses it to avoid redundant API calls when updating PR descriptions &mdash; if the hash hasn't changed, the description update is skipped.

---

## Nodes

A *node* is one branch (and its corresponding PR) within a stack. Nodes are ordered &mdash; the first node's parent is the stack base, and each subsequent node's parent is the node above it.

### Node status

Each node tracks its PR status. The possible values are:

| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `open` | The PR is open and under review. |
| `draft` | The PR is a draft, not yet ready for review. |
| `merged` | The PR has been merged into its base. |
| `closed` | The PR was closed without merging. |

### Merged nodes stay in the stack

When a node's PR merges, `sdf sync` does **not** remove it from the stack. Instead, the node remains in the stack JSON with status `"merged"`. The `ParentBranch()` function skips over merged nodes when computing the effective parent for downstream branches &mdash; so downstream nodes rebase onto the stack base (or the nearest non-merged ancestor) automatically.

This means merged PRs are shown as completed in the stack topology rather than silently disappearing.

---

## Configuration

SDF uses a two-tier configuration system:

- **Global config** &mdash; `~/.config/sdf/config.json`, user-specific defaults
- **Repo config** &mdash; `.sdf/config.json`, per-repo overrides

Repo config takes precedence over global config on a field-by-field basis. Run `sdf config show` to see the effective merged config.

```json
{
  "branch_prefix": {
    "enabled": true,
    "scope": "users-feature",
    "separator": "/"
  },
  "pr_title": {
    "conventional_commits": true,
    "ticket_pattern": ""
  },
  "sync": {
    "with_content": false
  }
}
```

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `branch_prefix.enabled` | bool | Whether new branches are auto-prefixed with the stack ID (default `true`). |
| `branch_prefix.scope` | string | Scope used as branch prefix and conventional commit scope. If empty, falls back to the stack ID. |
| `branch_prefix.separator` | string | Character between prefix and branch name (default `"/"`). |
| `pr_title.conventional_commits` | bool | Generate PR titles with conventional commit format using scope (default `true`). |
| `pr_title.ticket_pattern` | string | Regex to extract a ticket ID from the branch name for PR titles. |
| `sync.with_content` | bool | Whether `sdf sync` updates PR titles and descriptions (default `false`). |

---

## Repository layout

```
.sdf/                                       ← local-only (gitignored)
  config.json                               ← repo config
  stacks/
    users-feature.json                      ← stack topology
    auth-feature.json                       ← another stack
  local.json                                ← ephemeral state (sync progress, etc.)
```

The entire `.sdf/` directory is **local-only** &mdash; it is listed in `.gitignore` and is never pushed to the remote. Each developer's machine maintains its own copy of the stack metadata. PR descriptions on GitHub serve as the shared source of truth for stack structure and context.

---

## Stack resolution

When you run a command that operates on a stack (`sdf sync`, `sdf status`, `sdf branch`, etc.), SDF determines which stack to use with this logic:

1. **Explicit `--stack` flag** &mdash; always takes priority
2. **Positional argument** &mdash; e.g. `sdf sync my-feature`
3. **Current branch** &mdash; if your checked-out branch belongs to a stack, that stack is used
4. **Single stack** &mdash; if there's only one stack in the repo, it's used automatically

If none of these resolve to a stack (e.g. you're on `main` with multiple stacks and didn't specify one), SDF reports an error listing the available stacks. With [shell completions](/docs/getting-started#prerequisites) installed, you can tab-complete stack names directly &mdash; useful when working with multiple stacks.

---

## Local state

The file `.sdf/local.json` stores ephemeral state that should not be shared between developers:

- **Sync progress** &mdash; when a sync is paused for manual conflict resolution, the paused branch, resume index, and original branch are saved here. `sdf sync --continue` reads this to resume.
- **Split sessions** &mdash; maps stack names to Claude session IDs so split refinement can resume across invocations.

This file is automatically created when needed and can be safely deleted &mdash; SDF recreates it as necessary.

---

## Commands

Source: https://stacked-diffs-flow.com/docs/commands/

Full reference for every sdf command.

import CommandRef from '../../components/CommandRef.astro';
import cliRef from '../../data/cli-reference.json';

export const cmd = (name) => cliRef.commands.find(c => c.name === name);

# Commands

All commands are run from within a git repository. Most require the repository to have at least one stack registered (via `sdf new` or `sdf fetch`).

---

## Stack management

<CommandRef command={cmd('new')} />

<CommandRef command={cmd('fetch')} />

<CommandRef command={cmd('branch')} />

<CommandRef command={cmd('sync')} />

Steps performed:

1. Fetch from origin and fast-forward the base branch
2. Query GitHub for the status of each PR in the stack
3. Reconcile PR states (mark merged nodes, fill in PR numbers)
4. For each downstream node that needs rebasing: rebase onto new parent, push
5. Update PR base branches on GitHub when a merged node is skipped
6. Optionally update PR titles and descriptions (with `--with-content` or if configured)
7. Update stack navigation links in all PR descriptions

Merged nodes remain in the stack JSON and are displayed as completed. They are not removed. The `ParentBranch()` function skips merged nodes to find the effective parent for rebasing.

**Conflict resolution:** When a rebase conflict occurs, an interactive menu is presented with these options:

- **Ask Claude to resolve** (if `claude` CLI is available)
- **I'll fix it myself** &mdash; pauses sync; resume later with `sdf sync --continue`
- **Skip this branch** &mdash; aborts the rebase for this branch, continues with the rest
- **Abort sync** &mdash; stops the entire sync

After choosing "I'll fix it myself", resolve the conflicts manually, stage the files with `git add`, then run `sdf sync --continue`.

<CommandRef command={cmd('merge')} />

Merges the first open PR in the stack (the "head"), then runs `sdf sync` on the remaining branches. The safe pattern for draining a stack is to run `sdf merge` repeatedly &mdash; this keeps conflicts small by only crossing one squash boundary at a time. See the [Sync Deep Dive](/docs/sync-deep-dive#sdf-merge-vs-sdf-sync) for details.

<CommandRef command={cmd('status')} />

Fetches from origin and fast-forwards the base branch to ensure sync state is accurate. Shows each branch with its PR number, status (open/merged/closed), and whether it needs syncing. Also performs lightweight reconciliation against GitHub PR states and warns about structural drift.

<CommandRef command={cmd('pr')} />

<CommandRef command={cmd('move')} />

<CommandRef command={cmd('split')} />

Uses Claude to analyze the source branch's full diff, identify semantic themes, and propose a split plan. The plan groups changed files into layers ordered by dependency (types/schema first, then APIs, then business logic, then UI). Each layer becomes a branch in the new stack.

**Pipeline:**

1. **Analysis** &mdash; Claude groups changed files into layers by semantic theme. If a file spans multiple layers, a follow-up phase assigns individual hunks
2. **Plan** &mdash; SDF displays the split plan showing layers, files, and estimated diffs
3. **Review** &mdash; Interactive prompt to accept, refine (via Claude session), or abort
4. **Execute** &mdash; Creates branches by extracting per-layer diffs and applying them as patches. Shared files are split at the hunk level
5. **Validate** &mdash; Verifies `git diff original-branch stack/last-branch` is empty (lossless split)
6. **Ship** &mdash; Pushes branches, creates PRs with stack navigation links

**Plan refinement:** Choosing "Refine plan" opens a Claude session where you can give natural language instructions to adjust the split (move files between layers, merge layers, rename layers). SDF re-extracts the updated plan automatically.

**Safety:** The original branch is never modified. If validation fails, the split is rolled back. Use `--dry-run` to preview the plan without executing.
