## Configuration

Source: https://stacked-diffs-flow.com/docs/configuration/

Two-tier configuration for repos and individual users.

import ConfigRef from '../../components/ConfigRef.astro';
import cliRef from '../../data/cli-reference.json';

# Configuration

SDF uses a two-tier configuration system that separates team-wide settings from personal preferences.

---

## Config files

| File | Scope | Location |
|---|---|---|
| `.sdf/config.json` | Repository | Local-only (inside gitignored `.sdf/` directory) |
| `~/.config/sdf/config.json` | User (global) | Per-machine |

When both files exist, repository config takes precedence on a field-by-field basis. Missing files are not errors &mdash; SDF works without any config file, using built-in defaults.

Run `sdf config show` to see the effective merged result.

---

## Available settings

### `branch_prefix`

Controls automatic branch name prefixing when creating branches with `sdf branch`. This is a nested object with three sub-fields.

#### `branch_prefix.enabled`

Whether branch prefix enforcement is active.

- Type: `boolean`
- Default: `true`

#### `branch_prefix.scope`

The scope used as both the branch prefix and the conventional commit scope. When empty, falls back to the stack ID.

- Type: `string`
- Default: `""` (uses stack ID)

#### `branch_prefix.separator`

The character placed between the prefix and the branch name.

- Type: `string`
- Default: `"/"`

```json
{
  "branch_prefix": {
    "enabled": true,
    "scope": "team-name",
    "separator": "/"
  }
}
```

With this config, `sdf branch add-logging` creates `team-name/add-logging` instead of `add-logging`.

---

### `pr_title`

Controls how PR titles are generated. This is a nested object with two sub-fields.

#### `pr_title.conventional_commits`

PR titles follow the [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/) style, using the scope as the conventional commit scope (e.g., `feat(auth): add logging`).

- Type: `boolean`
- Default: `true`

#### `pr_title.ticket_pattern`

A regex pattern used to extract a ticket ID from the branch name and include it in the PR title.

- Type: `string`
- Default: `""` (disabled)

```json
{
  "pr_title": {
    "conventional_commits": true,
    "ticket_pattern": "[A-Z]+-[0-9]+"
  }
}
```

---

### `sync`

Controls behavior during `sdf sync`. This is a nested object.

#### `sync.with_content`

When enabled, `sdf sync` also updates PR titles and descriptions using Claude CLI.

- Type: `boolean`
- Default: `false`

```json
{
  "sync": {
    "with_content": true
  }
}
```

---

## Setting values

Use `sdf config set` to update individual keys. Valid keys are dot-separated paths into the config structure.

```bash
# Set in repo config (.sdf/config.json)
sdf config set branch_prefix.enabled true
sdf config set branch_prefix.scope team-name
sdf config set branch_prefix.separator /
sdf config set pr_title.conventional_commits false
sdf config set pr_title.ticket_pattern "[A-Z]+-[0-9]+"
sdf config set sync.with_content true

# Set in global config (~/.config/sdf/config.json)
sdf config set --global branch_prefix.scope my-username
```

Or edit the JSON files directly &mdash; they are plain JSON with no schema enforcement beyond what SDF reads.

### Valid keys

<ConfigRef keys={cliRef.config_keys} />

---

## Example repo config

```json
{
  "branch_prefix": {
    "enabled": true,
    "scope": "team-name",
    "separator": "/"
  },
  "pr_title": {
    "conventional_commits": true
  }
}
```

Save this as `.sdf/config.json` in any repo to use these settings. Since `.sdf/` is local-only, each developer creates this file on their own machine (or it is created automatically by `sdf new` and `sdf fetch`).

---

## Example global config

```json
{
  "branch_prefix": {
    "scope": "my-username"
  },
  "sync": {
    "with_content": true
  }
}
```

This lives in `~/.config/sdf/config.json` and applies to all repositories on your machine. Repo-level values override these on a field-by-field basis.

---

## AI Features

Source: https://stacked-diffs-flow.com/docs/ai-features/

How SDF uses Claude for branch splitting, conflict resolution, and PR content generation.

# AI Features

SDF integrates with the [Claude CLI](https://claude.ai/code) to provide three AI-powered capabilities: **branch splitting** via `sdf split`, **semantic conflict resolution** during sync and move operations, and **PR title and description generation**.

Conflict resolution and PR content generation are optional &mdash; without the Claude CLI installed, SDF falls back to manual conflict resolution and local title generation from branch names and commit subjects. Branch splitting requires the Claude CLI.

---

## Branch splitting

`sdf split` uses Claude as its analysis engine to decompose a large branch into a stack of focused PRs. This is the most AI-intensive feature in SDF &mdash; Claude is involved in every phase of the pipeline.

### File-level grouping

Claude receives the full diff and list of changed files between the base and source branches. It groups files into coherent layers &mdash; each representing a candidate PR &mdash; based on semantic themes: schema changes, API endpoints, business logic, UI components, etc.

A file typically appears in exactly one layer. When a file's changes clearly serve multiple concerns, it may appear in multiple layers &mdash; SDF handles this with hunk-level splitting in a follow-up phase.

### Dependency ordering

Claude determines the natural dependency order between layers: types and schemas before interfaces, APIs before business logic, business logic before UI. Tests travel with the code they test.

### Hunk-level splitting

When the same file contains changes from multiple themes, Claude assigns individual hunks to the appropriate layer. SDF validates these assignments against the actual diff to ensure every hunk is accounted for and no hunk appears in multiple layers.

### Plan refinement

After the initial plan is generated, you can open an interactive Claude session to refine it with natural language instructions. SDF re-extracts the updated plan and handles any shared file reassignment automatically.

### Session management

Split analysis uses a persistent Claude session named `split-analysis`. This session is reused during plan refinement, allowing Claude to maintain context across the full split workflow. The session ID is saved in `.sdf/local.json` so you can resume it later with `claude --resume <id>`.

---

## Semantic conflict resolution

When `sdf sync` triggers a cascade rebase and encounters a conflict, SDF presents an interactive menu:

1. **Ask Claude to resolve** (only shown if the Claude CLI is installed)
2. **I'll fix it myself (pauses sync)** &mdash; leaves the rebase in progress so you can resolve manually, then run `sdf sync --continue`
3. **Skip this branch** &mdash; aborts the rebase for this branch and continues with the rest of the stack
4. **Abort sync** &mdash; aborts the entire sync operation

If you choose Claude, SDF invokes it with:

1. **An upstream change diff summary** &mdash; a summary of what changed in the parent branch since the current branch was last rebased
2. **The current branch's PR description** &mdash; fetched from GitHub, used as context for what this branch is trying to do
3. **The conflicted file contents** &mdash; the full files with standard conflict markers (`<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>`)

Claude resolves each conflict file and writes the resolution back to disk. SDF then stages the files and runs `git rebase --continue`.

### Fallback behavior

If Claude's resolution fails (output cannot be parsed, or the rebase still fails after applying the resolution), SDF presents a second menu:

1. **I'll fix the rest myself (pauses sync)** &mdash; same as the manual resolution flow
2. **Skip this branch, continue with the rest**
3. **Abort sync entirely**

If the Claude CLI is not installed, the "Ask Claude to resolve" option is simply not shown in the menu.

### Conflict resolution during move

The `sdf move` command also uses Claude for conflict resolution. When cherry-picking or rebasing during a commit move encounters conflicts, SDF automatically invokes Claude (if available) with the same prompt structure: upstream diff summary, PR description, and conflicted file contents. If Claude fails, the rebase is aborted and you are asked to resolve manually.

---

## PR title and description generation

The `sdf sync --with-content` flag (or the `sync.with_content` config option) uses Claude to generate PR titles and descriptions for all open PRs in the stack.

```bash
# One-time flag
sdf sync --with-content

# Or set permanently in config
sdf config set sync.with_content true
```

When enabled, after the rebase phase completes, SDF processes each open PR in parallel:

### Title generation

Claude receives the branch name, commit subjects, and the full diff against the parent branch. It generates a short, descriptive title (under 60 characters, lowercase, no conventional commit prefix). SDF prepends the conventional commit prefix (e.g., `feat: `) if configured.

If the current title is already accurate, Claude is instructed to keep it unchanged. SDF also compares the proposed title against the existing one using word-level similarity and skips the update if they are close enough.

### Description generation

Claude receives the same inputs (branch, commits, diff) plus any existing description. It generates 2-5 sentences explaining what the change does and why. Descriptions are placed between `<!-- sdf:description -->` markers in the PR body, preserving any other content (like stack navigation links).

### Without Claude

If the Claude CLI is not installed, `--with-content` still updates PR titles using a local algorithm based on branch names and commit subjects. Description generation requires Claude and is skipped without it.

---

## Claude CLI sessions

SDF creates session names for Claude invocations using a dash-separated format:

```
conflict-feature-branch-name
pr-title-feature-branch-name
pr-desc-feature-branch-name
```

The prefix (`conflict`, `pr-title`, `pr-desc`) is determined by the call site. Branch names have slashes and spaces replaced with dashes. The session name is passed to `claude -p` for call-site clarity but is not currently used by the CLI for resumability.

---

## Teaching Claude about SDF

The `sdf ai intro` command spawns a Claude session that teaches Claude about SDF's commands, workflows, and conventions. Claude then creates a skill file so it remembers SDF context in future sessions:

```bash
sdf ai intro
```

This is useful when you want Claude to assist with SDF-managed repositories &mdash; after running `ai intro`, Claude understands stack topology, branch naming conventions, and how to use SDF commands correctly.

---

## AI and JSON mode

When `sdf sync --json` encounters a conflict, it cannot display the interactive resolution menu. Instead, the conflict is reported in the JSON output and the sync aborts. To use AI conflict resolution with automation, run `sdf sync` interactively first to resolve any conflicts, then use `--json` for subsequent scripted syncs.

---

## Installing the Claude CLI

```bash
# macOS
brew install claude

# Or download from
# https://claude.ai/code
```

Verify it's available:

```bash
sdf doctor
```

---

## Privacy and data

When SDF invokes Claude, it sends:

- **For branch splitting:** the full diff between base and source branch, and the list of changed files. For shared files (Phase 2), individual file diffs with numbered hunks
- **For conflict resolution:** upstream diff summaries, PR descriptions from GitHub, and file contents with conflict markers
- **For PR content generation:** branch diffs, commit subjects, and existing PR titles/descriptions

SDF does not send credentials, tokens, or any data outside your repository. The Claude CLI uses your existing Claude account and applies your account's data handling settings.

---

## Tips for better AI results

**Write good PR descriptions.** During conflict resolution, Claude receives the PR description as its primary context for understanding what your branch is trying to do. A description like "Adds users table" is less useful than "Adds the `users` table with columns `id`, `email`, `created_at`; uses `pgx/v5` driver; AppError pattern for DB errors."

**Document constraints in PR descriptions.** If a downstream branch depends on a specific function signature or interface from upstream, mention it in the PR description. Claude will use this to preserve it during conflict resolution.

**Review resolved files.** Claude's resolutions are good but not infallible. After a sync with AI-resolved conflicts, review the diff of each rebased branch before pushing.

**Review generated PR content.** Claude-generated titles and descriptions are a starting point. Review and edit them to ensure they accurately represent your changes.

---

## Sync Deep Dive

Source: https://stacked-diffs-flow.com/docs/sync-deep-dive/

How sdf sync works -- cascade rebase, reconciliation, conflict resolution, and PR updates.

# Sync Deep Dive

`sdf sync` is the core command in SDF. It detects what has changed on GitHub, rebases branches that need updating, pushes them, and updates PR metadata. This page explains every step in detail.

---

## The sync loop

When you run `sdf sync`, SDF executes this sequence:

1. **Fetch from origin** and fast-forward the base branch (e.g. `main`)
2. **Query GitHub** for the status of each PR in the stack
3. **Reconcile** PR states &mdash; mark merged nodes, fill in PR numbers, warn on drift
4. **Compute a sync plan** &mdash; determine which branches need rebasing
5. **Show the plan** and ask for confirmation (unless `-y`)
6. **Cascade rebase** each branch that needs updating, push, and update PR bases
7. **Offer to create PRs** for branches that don't have one
8. **Update PR content** &mdash; titles and descriptions (if `--with-content`)
9. **Update stack navigation** &mdash; the linked list of PRs in each PR description

---

## Step by step

### 1. Fetch and fast-forward

SDF runs `git fetch` to get the latest remote state, then fast-forwards the base branch (e.g. `origin/main → main`) so that local branch refs are current. If the fast-forward fails (e.g. local commits on main), SDF warns but continues.

### 2. Query GitHub for PR states

SDF calls `gh` to fetch the current state of every PR in the stack &mdash; open, merged, closed, plus the base branch and CI/review status. This is the data that drives reconciliation.

### 3. Reconcile

Reconciliation compares the local stack state (in `.sdf/stacks/<name>.json`) against what GitHub reports. Changes fall into two categories:

**Routine changes** are applied automatically and silently:
- A PR's status changed (e.g. `open → merged`) &mdash; the node is updated
- A PR number was discovered for a branch that had none &mdash; the number is filled in

**Notable changes** are displayed as warnings and require attention:
- A PR's base branch on GitHub doesn't match the expected parent in the stack
- A branch that was in the local stack is no longer in the PR chain on GitHub
- Branches have been reordered relative to the local stack

Notable changes are not applied automatically. If the drift is significant, use `sdf fetch` to re-discover the stack from GitHub's PR graph. Note that `sdf fetch` creates a **new local stack** to track the discovered PR chain &mdash; it does not modify the existing stack in place. You may need to remove the stale stack manually after verifying the fetched one is correct.

### 4. Compute the sync plan

SDF walks the stack from bottom to top. For each non-merged node, it compares the node's `base_tip` (the commit hash of the parent branch at the time of the last sync) against the current tip of the parent branch. If they differ, the branch needs rebasing.

The plan is a list of actions:
- **skip-merged** &mdash; acknowledge that a node's PR was merged (no rebase needed)
- **rebase** &mdash; the parent branch has moved; this branch needs `git rebase --onto`
- **update-pr-base** &mdash; the PR's base branch on GitHub needs changing (because a merged node was skipped)

### 5. Cascade rebase

This is the core operation. For each branch that needs rebasing, SDF runs:

```
git rebase --onto <new-parent-tip> <old-base-tip> <branch>
```

The `--onto` form is critical. It tells git: "take the commits unique to `<branch>` (those after `<old-base-tip>`) and replay them on top of `<new-parent-tip>`." This cleanly handles the case where the parent branch has been rebased or squash-merged.

After a successful rebase, SDF:
- Updates the node's `base_tip` to the new parent tip
- Force-pushes the branch with `--force-with-lease`
- Updates the PR's base branch on GitHub if the parent branch name changed (e.g. when a merged node is skipped, downstream PRs need their base changed from the merged branch to the next open branch or to `main`)

#### How `base_tip` works

Every node in the stack stores a `base_tip` &mdash; the commit SHA at the tip of its parent branch at the time of the last sync. This is how SDF knows whether a branch is "in sync" or "needs sync":

```
Before sync:
  main (tip: abc123)
    └─ auth (base_tip: abc123, in sync)
        └─ api (base_tip: def456, in sync)

After a commit is pushed to auth:
  main (tip: abc123)
    └─ auth (tip: ghi789)  ← new commits
        └─ api (base_tip: def456)  ← stale! parent moved
```

When SDF syncs, it rebases `api` onto the new tip of `auth`, then updates `api`'s `base_tip` to `ghi789`.

#### What happens when a PR merges

When the bottom PR in a stack merges (e.g. `auth` merges into `main`), the stack topology changes:

```
Before:
  main ← auth (merged) ← api ← ui

After sync:
  main ← api ← ui
```

SDF detects the merge during reconciliation, marks the node as `merged`, then rebases `api` onto `main` (skipping the merged `auth` node). It also runs `gh pr edit <api-PR> --base main` to update the PR's base on GitHub &mdash; without this step, GitHub would show every commit from `main` in the PR diff.

The `ParentBranch()` function handles this transparently: it walks backward through the node list, skipping merged nodes, until it finds an open node or reaches the base branch.

### 6. Conflict resolution

When a rebase produces conflicts, SDF presents an interactive menu with four options:

**Claude resolution** &mdash; SDF builds a prompt containing the upstream change summary, the PR description from GitHub, and the full content of every conflicted file (with conflict markers). Claude resolves the conflicts in place, SDF stages the resolved files, and the rebase continues. If Claude fails to produce valid resolutions, SDF falls back to the other options.

**Manual resolution (pause)** &mdash; SDF saves the sync progress to `.sdf/local.json` and exits. You resolve the conflicts in your editor, stage the files, and run `sdf sync --continue` to resume. The saved state includes which branch was paused, which node index to resume from, and which branch you were on before the sync started.

**Skip branch** &mdash; SDF aborts the rebase for this branch and continues with the rest of the stack. Branches that depend on the skipped branch are also skipped (blocked). Run `sdf sync` again later to retry.

**Abort** &mdash; SDF aborts the rebase and stops the sync entirely. No branches are left in a partial state.

### 7. Offer to create missing PRs

After the rebase phase, SDF checks for open branches that don't have a PR yet. For each one, it prompts you to create a PR. If you accept, SDF pushes the branch and runs `gh pr create` with an auto-generated title.

### 8. Update PR content

If `--with-content` is passed (or `sync.with_content` is set to `true` in config), SDF updates the title and description of every open PR in the stack:

- **Titles** are generated from conventional commit subjects (if enabled) or branch names. If Claude is available, it generates titles from the diff. SDF uses a similarity threshold (Jaccard similarity of 0.8) to avoid noisy updates when the title hasn't meaningfully changed.
- **Descriptions** are generated by Claude from the branch diff and commit messages. A higher similarity threshold (0.85) prevents unnecessary updates.

Title and description updates run in parallel across all PRs for speed.

### 9. Update stack navigation

SDF maintains a navigation section in each PR description that shows the full stack with links to every PR. After sync, it updates these navigation links in all PRs. A content hash prevents unnecessary GitHub API calls when nothing has changed.

---

## `sdf sync --continue`

When a sync was paused for manual conflict resolution, `--continue` resumes it. SDF checks three conditions:

1. **Rebase still in progress** &mdash; runs `git rebase --continue` (you must have staged all resolved files first)
2. **Rebase completed externally** &mdash; if the parent tip is an ancestor of the paused branch, the rebase was completed outside SDF (e.g. you ran `git rebase --continue` manually). SDF acknowledges this and continues.
3. **Rebase was aborted** &mdash; if the parent tip is NOT an ancestor, the rebase was aborted. SDF clears the saved progress and starts a fresh sync.

After handling the paused branch, SDF resumes the sync loop from the next node.

---

## `sdf merge` vs. `sdf sync`

`sdf merge` combines merging and syncing into a single safe operation:

1. Finds the first open PR in the stack (the "head")
2. Retargets the next PR's base to the stack base (prevents GitHub from auto-closing it when the head branch is deleted)
3. Merges the head PR via `gh pr merge` (default: squash)
4. Marks the node as merged
5. Runs a full `sdf sync` on the remaining branches

The key insight from the [squash-merge conflict cascade](/docs/case-studies/squash-merge-conflict-cascade) case study: merging one PR at a time and syncing after each merge keeps conflicts small. Batch-merging multiple PRs creates a cascade of conflicts because downstream branches were written on top of incremental history that no longer exists after squashing.

**Best practice:** Use `sdf merge` repeatedly to drain a stack from the bottom up, rather than merging PRs directly on GitHub.

---

## Flags reference

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--yes`, `-y` | Skip the confirmation prompt |
| `--continue` | Resume after manual conflict resolution |
| `--with-content` | Update PR titles and descriptions (can also be set via config) |
| `--stack <name>` | Specify which stack to sync (default: auto-detect from current branch) |
| `--json` | Output structured JSON result (implies `--yes`, aborts on conflict) |

---

## Splitting Branches

Source: https://stacked-diffs-flow.com/docs/splitting-branches/

How to use sdf split to decompose a large branch into a stack of focused PRs.

# Splitting Branches

`sdf split` takes a large branch and decomposes it into a stack of smaller, focused PRs. Claude analyzes the diff and proposes a split plan &mdash; grouping files by theme, ordering layers by dependency, and handling shared files at the hunk level. The original branch is never modified.

---

## When to use split

Use `sdf split` when you have an existing branch with a large diff that should have been a stack from the start. Common scenarios:

- A feature branch grew to 2,000+ lines and reviewers are struggling
- You prototyped something in a single branch and want to submit it as reviewable layers
- You inherited a branch from someone else and need to break it down

If you're starting fresh, use `sdf new` and `sdf branch` to build the stack incrementally. Split is for after-the-fact decomposition.

---

## Prerequisites

- **Claude CLI** &mdash; required. Split uses Claude for analysis, plan generation, and hunk assignment. Install from [claude.ai/code](https://claude.ai/code).
- **Clean working tree** &mdash; no uncommitted changes
- **Source branch must not already be in a stack**
- **Source branch must have 2+ changed files** relative to the base

---

## Basic usage

```bash
sdf split --from feature/big-change --stack my-feature
```

Required flags:
- `--from <branch>` &mdash; the source branch to split
- `--stack <name>` &mdash; the name for the new stack that will hold the split layers

Optional flags:
- `--base <branch>` &mdash; base branch (default: auto-detected from `origin/HEAD`)
- `--dry-run` &mdash; show the plan without executing
- `--yes`, `-y` &mdash; skip the confirmation prompt
- `--no-push` &mdash; create branches locally without pushing or creating PRs

---

## How it works

### Phase 1: Analysis

Claude receives the full diff between the base branch and the source branch, including the list of changed files, commit log, and file tree. It groups the files into coherent layers &mdash; each representing a candidate PR &mdash; based on semantic themes.

For example, a feature branch touching database migrations, API endpoints, business logic, and tests might be split into:

```
Layer 1: Database schema (3 files, +120 -0)
  Migration and model definitions

Layer 2: API endpoints (5 files, +340 -20)
  HTTP handlers and route registration

Layer 3: Business logic (4 files, +280 -15)
  Service layer and validation

Layer 4: Tests (6 files, +450 -0)
  Unit and integration tests
```

Each file typically appears in exactly one layer. When a file's changes serve multiple concerns, it may appear in multiple layers &mdash; SDF handles this in the hunk assignment phase.

### Phase 2: Dependency ordering

Claude determines the natural dependency order between layers. Types and schemas come before interfaces, APIs before business logic, business logic before UI. Tests travel with the code they test. The ordering ensures each layer compiles and passes tests independently.

### Phase 3: Display and decision

After analysis, SDF displays the split plan showing each layer's name, description, file count, and line statistics. You then choose one of three actions:

- **Execute** &mdash; proceed with the split as proposed
- **Refine** &mdash; open an interactive Claude session to adjust the plan with natural language instructions (e.g., "move the validation files to layer 2" or "merge layers 3 and 4")
- **Abort** &mdash; cancel the split

### Phase 4: Hunk-level splitting (if needed)

When the same file appears in multiple layers (shared files), SDF assigns individual diff hunks to the appropriate layer. Claude examines each hunk and assigns it based on its semantic content. SDF validates that every hunk is accounted for and no hunk appears in multiple layers.

If hunk assignment fails (Claude can't produce valid assignments), SDF falls back to keeping each shared file in its first layer only.

### Phase 5: Execution

SDF creates the stack and branches:

1. Initializes the stack with `sdf new`
2. For each layer, creates a branch and applies the layer's changes
3. Validates tree identity &mdash; confirms that the tip of the last branch is identical to the source branch (lossless split)
4. Pushes all branches to origin
5. Creates PRs for each branch with auto-generated titles

If validation fails (the split is not lossless), SDF rolls back &mdash; deletes the created branches and stack &mdash; and reports the error.

### Phase 6: Session management

The Claude session ID is saved in `.sdf/local.json` so you can resume the analysis session later:

```bash
claude --resume <session-id>
```

The session ID is displayed at the end of the split output.

---

## Worked example

```bash
# You have a large branch with 15 changed files
$ sdf split --from feature/user-management --stack users

Analyzing feature/user-management...

Split plan for users (base: main)
──────────────────────────────────────────────────

  Layer 1: Database models (3 files, +145 -0)
    User and role table migrations, model structs

  Layer 2: Repository layer (4 files, +230 -12)
    CRUD operations for users and roles

  Layer 3: API handlers (5 files, +380 -25)
    REST endpoints for user management

  Layer 4: Integration tests (3 files, +290 -0)
    End-to-end tests for all endpoints

  Total: 15 files across 4 layers

? What would you like to do?
  > Execute this split
    Refine plan (opens Claude session)
    Abort
```

After execution:

```
  ✓ Layer 1: users/database-models -- 3 files applied
  ✓ Layer 2: users/repository-layer -- 4 files applied
  ✓ Layer 3: users/api-handlers -- 5 files applied
  ✓ Layer 4: users/integration-tests -- 3 files applied
  ✓ Tree identity verified -- split is lossless

Pushing branches to origin...
  ✓ users/database-models
  ✓ users/repository-layer
  ✓ users/api-handlers
  ✓ users/integration-tests

Creating pull requests...
  ✓ PR #201: users/database-models → main
  ✓ PR #202: users/repository-layer → users/database-models
  ✓ PR #203: users/api-handlers → users/repository-layer
  ✓ PR #204: users/integration-tests → users/api-handlers

✓ Split complete -- 4 branches created in stack "users"
```

---

## Refining the plan

If the initial plan isn't quite right, choose "Refine plan" to open an interactive Claude session. You can give natural language instructions:

- "Move `internal/validation.go` from layer 3 to layer 2"
- "Merge layers 2 and 3 into a single layer"
- "Split the tests into their own layer"
- "Rename layer 1 to 'Schema changes'"

After you exit the Claude session (`/exit`), SDF re-extracts the updated plan and handles any shared file reassignment automatically.

---

## Dry run

Use `--dry-run` to see the plan without executing:

```bash
sdf split --from feature/big-change --stack my-feature --dry-run
```

This runs the full analysis phase and displays the plan, but does not create any branches, push, or create PRs.

---

## Local-only split

Use `--no-push` to create branches locally without pushing or creating PRs:

```bash
sdf split --from feature/big-change --stack my-feature --no-push
```

You can then inspect the branches locally, push them manually, and create PRs with `sdf pr` from each branch.

---

## What can go wrong

**Analysis fails:** If Claude can't produce a valid split plan, the command fails without modifying anything.

**Validation fails (not lossless):** If the final tree doesn't match the source branch exactly, SDF rolls back all created branches and the stack. This means a bug in the splitting logic &mdash; report it.

**Hunk assignment fails:** If shared files can't be split at the hunk level, SDF falls back to keeping each shared file in whichever layer it first appears. The split may still be valid, but some files might not land in their ideal layer.

**Push fails:** If pushing fails for some branches, SDF skips PR creation and tells you to push manually, then create PRs with `sdf pr`.

---

## Multiple Stacks

Source: https://stacked-diffs-flow.com/docs/multiple-stacks/

Managing several independent stacks in a single repository.

# Multiple Stacks

A single repository can have multiple independent stacks, each with its own base branch and set of branches. This is useful when you're working on several features in parallel.

---

## Creating multiple stacks

Each `sdf new` call creates a separate stack:

```bash
# First stack: authentication feature
sdf new auth-feature --branch login-page
# ... work on auth ...
sdf branch session-api
sdf branch logout

# Second stack: billing feature
sdf new billing --branch models
# ... work on billing ...
sdf branch stripe-integration
```

You now have two independent stacks:

```
auth-feature (base: main)
  └─ auth-feature/login-page
      └─ auth-feature/session-api
          └─ auth-feature/logout

billing (base: main)
  └─ billing/models
      └─ billing/stripe-integration
```

Each stack has its own JSON file in `.sdf/stacks/`:

```
.sdf/
  stacks/
    auth-feature.json
    billing.json
```

---

## Stack resolution

When you run a command like `sdf sync`, `sdf status`, or `sdf branch`, SDF needs to know which stack you mean. It resolves the stack using this logic:

1. **Explicit flag** &mdash; if you pass `--stack <name>`, that stack is used
2. **Positional argument** &mdash; for commands that accept it (e.g., `sdf sync auth-feature`)
3. **Current branch** &mdash; if your current branch belongs to a stack, that stack is used
4. **Single stack** &mdash; if there's only one stack in the repo, it's used automatically

If none of these apply (e.g., you're on `main` with multiple stacks), SDF asks you to specify:

```
$ sdf status
Error: multiple stacks found -- specify one with --stack <name> or switch to a stack branch

Available stacks:
  auth-feature  (3 branches)
  billing       (2 branches)
```

---

## Switching between stacks

Use `sdf switch` to navigate:

```bash
# List all branches across all stacks
$ sdf switch

# Switch to a specific branch
$ sdf switch auth-feature/login-page

# Shorthand -- omit "switch" when the argument contains a "/"
$ sdf auth-feature/login-page
```

When you run `sdf switch` without arguments, it lists every branch from every stack, grouped by stack, with the current branch marked:

```
$ sdf switch

auth-feature (base: main)
  → auth-feature/login-page     PR #12  open
    auth-feature/session-api    PR #13  open
    auth-feature/logout         PR #14  open

billing (base: main)
    billing/models              PR #15  open
    billing/stripe-integration  PR #16  open
```

---

## Syncing specific stacks

When you're on a branch that belongs to a stack, `sdf sync` syncs that stack automatically. To sync a different stack:

```bash
# Sync by name
sdf sync auth-feature

# Or use the flag
sdf sync --stack billing
```

---

## Different base branches

Stacks can have different base branches:

```bash
sdf new hotfix-stack --base release/v2.1 --branch fix-crash
sdf new feature-stack --base main --branch new-widget
```

Each stack's sync operates independently against its own base branch.

---

## Branch uniqueness

A branch can only belong to one stack. If you try to add a branch that already exists in another stack, SDF reports an error:

```
Error: branch "shared-utils" is already in stack "auth-feature"
```

This prevents ambiguity in stack resolution and ensures each branch has a clear home.

---

## Checking status across stacks

To see the status of a specific stack:

```bash
sdf status auth-feature
sdf status billing
```

Or switch to any branch in the stack and run `sdf status` without arguments.

---

## Fetching & Reconciliation

Source: https://stacked-diffs-flow.com/docs/fetching-stacks/

How to import existing PR stacks from GitHub and keep local state in sync.

# Fetching & Reconciliation

`sdf fetch` discovers PR stacks on GitHub and imports them into your local SDF metadata. This is essential for two scenarios: onboarding a second developer onto an existing stack, and rebuilding local state after it's lost (e.g., cloning a repo where stacks were already created).

---

## Discovering stacks

When you run `sdf fetch`, SDF:

1. Lists all your open PRs via `gh`
2. Builds a dependency graph from the PR base/head relationships
3. Finds chains of 2 or more PRs where each PR's base is the previous PR's head
4. Presents the discovered stacks for you to select

```bash
$ sdf fetch

Scanning your open PRs (base: main)...

Found 1 potential stack(s):

  [1] base: main
      ├─ #142  users-feature/db-schema
      ├─ #143  users-feature/repository
      └─ #144  users-feature/controller

? Fetch this stack? (Y/n)
```

A single PR targeting `main` is not a stack &mdash; discovery requires at least 2 chained PRs.

---

## First-time registration

If the discovered stack doesn't match any existing local stack, SDF registers it as a new stack:

1. Creates `.sdf/stacks/<name>.json` with nodes from the PR chain
2. Infers the stack name from branch prefixes (e.g., branches starting with `users-feature/` become stack `users-feature`)
3. Detects branch prefix configuration (separator style, scope) and creates `.sdf/config.json` if needed
4. Fetches all branches from origin so they exist locally

After registration, you can use `sdf sync`, `sdf status`, `sdf branch`, and all other commands normally.

---

## Reconciliation

If the discovered stack matches an existing local stack (by branch overlap), SDF reconciles the differences instead of creating a duplicate.

Reconciliation compares local state against what GitHub reports and classifies each difference:

### Routine changes (applied automatically)

- **Status updates** &mdash; a PR moved from `open` to `merged` or `closed`
- **PR number fills** &mdash; a branch that had no PR number locally now has one on GitHub

These are applied silently and save you from having to manually update the stack JSON.

### Notable changes (displayed as warnings)

- **Base branch changed** &mdash; the stack's base branch differs between local and GitHub
- **Branch reordered** &mdash; a branch moved to a different position in the chain
- **Branch removed** &mdash; a branch in the local stack is no longer in the PR chain on GitHub
- **Branch inserted** &mdash; a new branch appeared mid-stack that wasn't there locally
- **Base mismatch** &mdash; a PR's base on GitHub doesn't match the expected parent in the local stack
- **PR missing** &mdash; a PR number is recorded locally but the PR no longer exists on GitHub

Notable changes are surfaced as warnings during `sdf sync` and `sdf status`. They are not applied automatically because they may indicate unexpected drift that requires human judgment.

---

## Using fetch in a team

When multiple developers work with SDF on the same repository, each maintains their own local `.sdf/` directory. The workflow for a second developer joining an existing stack:

```bash
# Clone the repo
git clone https://github.com/org/repo.git
cd repo

# Install sdf
brew install pavelpascari/tap/sdf

# Discover and import existing stacks
sdf fetch

# Now work with the stack normally
sdf status
sdf sync
```

Since `.sdf/` is local-only (gitignored), there is no coordination needed between developers' SDF installations. Each developer independently discovers the stack from the PR graph.

---

## Flags

| Flag | Effect |
|---|---|
| `--stack <name>` | Name the stack explicitly (default: auto-inferred from branch prefixes) |
| `--base <branch>` | Specify the base branch for discovery (default: auto-detected from `origin/HEAD`) |
| `--json` | Output structured JSON result |

---

## When fetch doesn't find your PRs

See the [troubleshooting guide](/docs/troubleshooting#sdf-fetch-doesnt-find-my-prs) for common causes and fixes.

---

## JSON Output & Scripting

Source: https://stacked-diffs-flow.com/docs/json-output/

Using sdf's --json flag for automation, CI pipelines, and AI agent integration.

# JSON Output & Scripting

Every major SDF command supports a `--json` flag that outputs structured JSON instead of human-readable terminal output. This enables integration with CI pipelines, shell scripts, and AI agents.

---

## Commands with JSON support

| Command | Flag | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `sdf new` | `--json` | |
| `sdf branch` | `--json` | |
| `sdf status` | `--json` | |
| `sdf sync` | `--json` | Implies `--yes`; aborts on conflict |
| `sdf merge` | `--json` | Requires `--yes` |
| `sdf pr` | `--json` | |
| `sdf move` | `--json` | |
| `sdf fetch` | `--json` | Auto-selects if one stack found |
| `sdf switch` | `--json` | |
| `sdf config show` | `--json` | |
| `sdf config set` | `--json` | |
| `sdf doctor` | `--json` | |

---

## Output shapes

### sdf new --json

```json
{
  "stack": "my-feature",
  "base": "main",
  "branch": "my-feature/my-feature",
  "pushed": true
}
```

### sdf branch --json

```json
{
  "branch": "my-feature/api-layer",
  "stack": "my-feature",
  "parent": "my-feature/db-schema"
}
```

### sdf status --json

```json
{
  "stack": "my-feature",
  "base": "main",
  "current_branch": "my-feature/api-layer",
  "nodes": [
    {
      "branch": "my-feature/db-schema",
      "pr": 142,
      "status": "merged",
      "sync_state": "in_sync"
    },
    {
      "branch": "my-feature/api-layer",
      "pr": 143,
      "status": "open",
      "sync_state": "needs_sync",
      "commits_ahead": 3,
      "is_current": true,
      "ci_status": "success",
      "review_status": "approved",
      "mergeable": "mergeable"
    }
  ],
  "needs_sync": ["my-feature/api-layer"]
}
```

### sdf sync --json

```json
{
  "stack": "my-feature",
  "base": "main",
  "branches": [
    {
      "branch": "my-feature/db-schema",
      "pr": 142,
      "action": "merged"
    },
    {
      "branch": "my-feature/api-layer",
      "pr": 143,
      "action": "rebased",
      "pushed": true,
      "base_updated": true
    }
  ],
  "pr_updates": [
    { "pr": 143, "field": "title", "status": "updated" }
  ]
}
```

Possible `action` values: `"merged"`, `"rebased"`, `"in_sync"`, `"failed"`, `"blocked"`.

### sdf merge --json

```json
{
  "stack": "my-feature",
  "merged_pr": 142,
  "merged_branch": "my-feature/db-schema",
  "method": "squash",
  "base": "main",
  "retargeted_pr": 143,
  "remaining": 2
}
```

### sdf pr --json

```json
{
  "number": 145,
  "url": "https://github.com/org/repo/pull/145",
  "title": "feat(my-feature): add API endpoints"
}
```

### sdf move --json

```json
{
  "source": "my-feature/api-layer",
  "target": "my-feature/db-schema",
  "commits": ["abc1234", "def5678"]
}
```

### sdf fetch --json

```json
{
  "stack": "my-feature",
  "base": "main",
  "nodes": [
    { "branch": "my-feature/db-schema", "pr": 142 },
    { "branch": "my-feature/api-layer", "pr": 143 }
  ],
  "action": "registered"
}
```

Possible `action` values: `"registered"`, `"reconciled"`, `"up_to_date"`.

### sdf switch --json

```json
{
  "branch": "my-feature/api-layer",
  "stack": "my-feature",
  "layer": 2,
  "total": 3
}
```

### sdf doctor --json

```json
{
  "dependencies": [
    { "name": "git", "found": true, "version": "2.43.0", "path": "/usr/bin/git", "required": true },
    { "name": "gh", "found": true, "version": "2.40.1", "path": "/usr/bin/gh", "required": false },
    { "name": "claude", "found": false, "required": false }
  ],
  "ok": true
}
```

---

## Scripting examples

### Check if sync is needed

```bash
needs_sync=$(sdf status --json | jq -r '.needs_sync | length')
if [ "$needs_sync" -gt 0 ]; then
  echo "Stack needs sync"
  sdf sync -y
fi
```

### Get the current branch's PR number

```bash
pr=$(sdf status --json | jq -r '.nodes[] | select(.is_current) | .pr')
echo "Current PR: #$pr"
```

### Check all CI statuses

```bash
sdf status --json | jq -r '.nodes[] | select(.status == "open") | "\(.branch): CI=\(.ci_status) Review=\(.review_status)"'
```

### Merge the head PR and report

```bash
result=$(sdf merge --json --yes)
merged=$(echo "$result" | jq -r '.merged_pr')
remaining=$(echo "$result" | jq -r '.remaining')
echo "Merged PR #$merged, $remaining remaining"
```

---

## Gotchas

**`sdf sync --json` aborts on conflict.** Since JSON mode cannot display the interactive conflict resolution menu, any rebase conflict causes an immediate abort. The error is included in the JSON output as the `error` field. Run `sdf sync` without `--json` to resolve conflicts interactively.

**`sdf merge --json` requires `--yes`.** The merge command requires explicit confirmation in JSON mode since it performs a destructive operation.

**`sdf fetch --json` with multiple stacks.** If `sdf fetch` discovers multiple stacks and `--json` is specified, it returns an error. Use `--base` to narrow the results to one stack.

**Errors in JSON output.** When a command fails in JSON mode, the error is included in the JSON output as an `error` field rather than being printed to stderr. The command still exits with code 0 so the JSON can be parsed.

---

## Troubleshooting

Source: https://stacked-diffs-flow.com/docs/troubleshooting/

Common errors, recovery procedures, and how to get unstuck.

# Troubleshooting

This page covers common error states and how to recover from them. Headers match the error messages you'll see in your terminal so you can search for them directly.

---

## "working tree is not clean"

**When it happens:** Running `sdf sync`, `sdf move`, or `sdf split` with uncommitted changes.

**Fix:** Commit or stash your changes before running the command:

```bash
git stash
sdf sync
git stash pop
```

---

## "a rebase is in progress from a previous sync pause"

**When it happens:** Running `sdf sync` when a previous sync was paused for manual conflict resolution and the rebase was never completed or aborted.

**Fix &mdash; if you want to continue resolving:**

```bash
# Resolve the remaining conflicts in your editor
git add <resolved-files>
sdf sync --continue
```

**Fix &mdash; if you want to start over:**

```bash
git rebase --abort
sdf sync
```

---

## "no paused sync to continue"

**When it happens:** Running `sdf sync --continue` when there is no paused sync to resume.

**Fix:** Run `sdf sync` without `--continue` to start a fresh sync.

---

## "rebase --continue failed"

**When it happens:** Running `sdf sync --continue` when not all conflicts have been resolved, or resolved files haven't been staged.

**Fix:**

```bash
# Check which files still have conflicts
git diff --name-only --diff-filter=U

# Resolve them, then stage
git add <resolved-files>

# Resume
sdf sync --continue
```

---

## Claude failed to resolve a conflict

**When it happens:** During `sdf sync`, Claude attempts to resolve a rebase conflict but produces output that can't be applied. The interactive menu reappears with the same four options.

**What to do:**

1. **Try manual resolution.** Choose "Resolve manually" from the menu. SDF pauses the sync and saves progress. Resolve the conflicts in your editor, stage the files, and run `sdf sync --continue`.

2. **Skip the branch.** If you don't need this branch right now, choose "Skip branch." The branch stays unrebased and SDF continues with the rest of the stack. You can retry later with `sdf sync`.

3. **Abort.** Choose "Abort" to stop the sync entirely. No branches are left in a partial state.

---

## I merged multiple PRs on GitHub without running sync between each

**What happens:** When several PRs are squash-merged at once, downstream branches were written on top of incremental commit history that no longer exists in the squashed main branch. The rebase may produce many conflicts because git can't match context lines across multiple squash boundaries.

**How to recover:**

1. Run `sdf sync`. It will attempt to rebase the remaining branches.
2. If Claude can resolve the conflicts, the sync completes normally.
3. If conflicts are too large, resolve them manually or abort and consider the `sdf merge` workflow going forward.

**How to prevent this:** Use `sdf merge` to merge one PR at a time. It merges the head PR, runs sync automatically, and keeps conflicts small and manageable.

```bash
sdf merge              # merges the first open PR, then syncs
# wait for CI, then:
sdf merge              # merges the next one
```

---

## I merged PRs out of order on GitHub

**What happens:** If PR #2 in a stack is merged before PR #1, `sdf sync` detects the merge via GitHub and attempts to rebase. The result depends on how much the out-of-order merge overlaps with other branches.

**How to recover:**

1. Run `sdf sync`. It will reconcile the PR states from GitHub and attempt the cascade rebase.
2. Expect conflicts if the merged PR's changes overlap with branches that assumed a different order.
3. Resolve conflicts manually or with Claude's assistance.

**How to prevent this:** Merge from the bottom of the stack upward, one at a time.

---

## My local stack state is out of sync with GitHub

**What happens:** The local `.sdf/stacks/<name>.json` shows different PR numbers, statuses, or branch order than what exists on GitHub. This can happen if someone else modified PRs, or if you made changes on a different machine.

**How to recover:**

Run `sdf sync`. The first thing sync does is query GitHub for PR states and reconcile:

- **Routine changes** (status updates, PR number fills) are applied automatically.
- **Notable changes** (base mismatches, reorders, missing PRs) are displayed as warnings.

If the drift is severe, use `sdf fetch` to re-discover the stack from the GitHub PR graph:

```bash
sdf fetch
```

This scans all open PRs for branch chains and lets you re-register the stack.

---

## I deleted .sdf/ accidentally

**How to recover:** Use `sdf fetch` to rebuild the stack from GitHub's PR graph:

```bash
sdf fetch
```

SDF scans open PRs, discovers branch chains (sequences of 2+ PRs where each PR's base is the previous PR's head), and creates the local stack metadata. Your PRs and branches on GitHub are not affected &mdash; only local metadata was lost.

---

## `sdf fetch` doesn't find my PRs

**Possible causes:**

1. **PRs are not chained.** `sdf fetch` looks for chains of 2 or more PRs where each PR's base branch is the head branch of the previous PR. A single PR targeting `main` is not a stack.

2. **PRs are closed or merged.** `sdf fetch` only scans open PRs. Merged PRs won't appear in the discovery.

3. **`gh` is not authenticated.** Run `gh auth status` to verify your GitHub authentication.

4. **Base branch detection.** If your stack is based on a branch other than the default (e.g., `develop` instead of `main`), try specifying it:

```bash
sdf fetch --base develop
```

---

## "conflict in &lt;branch&gt; &mdash; cannot resolve in --json mode"

**When it happens:** Running `sdf sync --json` when a rebase conflict occurs. JSON mode cannot display the interactive conflict resolution menu.

**Fix:** Run `sdf sync` without `--json` to get the interactive conflict resolution options, or use `sdf sync --json --yes` and handle conflicts after the sync reports them.

---

## Branch is not in any stack

**When it happens:** Running a stack command while on a branch that isn't registered in any stack.

**Fix:** Switch to a branch that is part of a stack, or specify the stack explicitly:

```bash
sdf status --stack my-feature
sdf sync --stack my-feature
```

If the branch should be part of a stack but isn't, add it:

```bash
sdf switch <existing-stack-branch>
sdf branch <new-branch-name>
```

---

## Push failed after rebase

**When it happens:** During `sdf sync`, the force-push (`git push --force-with-lease`) fails for a branch. This usually means someone else pushed to the branch since the last fetch.

**How to recover:**

1. SDF reports the push failure as a warning and continues syncing other branches.
2. After sync completes, fetch and try pushing manually:

```bash
git fetch origin
git push --force-with-lease origin <branch-name>
```

---

## sdf doctor reports missing dependencies

Run `sdf doctor` to check which dependencies are available:

```bash
sdf doctor
```

| Dependency | Required? | What it's needed for |
|---|---|---|
| `git` | Yes | All operations |
| `gh` | No (but recommended) | PR creation, base updates, status checks |
| `claude` | No | AI conflict resolution, `sdf split`, PR content generation |

**Install missing dependencies:**

```bash
# git (usually pre-installed)
# macOS: xcode-select --install
# Linux: sudo apt install git

# GitHub CLI
brew install gh
gh auth login

# Claude CLI (optional)
# See https://claude.ai/code for installation instructions
```

---

## General recovery: starting fresh

If your local state is thoroughly broken and you want to start over without affecting anything on GitHub:

```bash
# Remove local SDF metadata
rm -rf .sdf/

# Re-discover stacks from GitHub
sdf fetch
```

Your branches, PRs, and code on GitHub are not affected. Only the local `.sdf/` directory is rebuilt.

---

## Moving Commits

Source: https://stacked-diffs-flow.com/docs/moving-commits/

How to use sdf move to relocate commits from the current branch to its parent.

# Moving Commits Between Branches

`sdf move` relocates commits from the current branch to its parent in the stack. This is useful when you realize work belongs in a different PR, or when you want to split a large branch into smaller, reviewable pieces.

---

## Basic usage: move to parent

Move commits from the current branch down to its parent:

```bash
# You're on feature/api with commits [a1, a2, a3]
# Stack: main ← feature/auth ← feature/api

sdf move a1 a2
```

This:
1. Cherry-picks `a1` and `a2` onto `feature/auth`
2. Rebases `feature/api` to strip the moved commits
3. Cascade-rebases any downstream branches
4. Updates the stack state

**Constraints:**
- Commits must be a contiguous prefix (oldest-first) of the branch
- At least one commit must remain on the source branch
- Working tree must be clean

---

## Splitting a branch into a new branch

When you want to extract commits into a **new** branch (not the existing parent), combine `sdf branch` with `sdf move`:

### Pattern: extract work into a new child branch

```bash
# Current stack: main ← feature/auth [a1, a2, a3, a4, a5]
# You realize a4 and a5 are a separate concern

# 1. Create a new branch (appended to stack)
sdf branch api-layer

# 2. Switch back to the source branch
sdf switch feature/auth

# 3. Move the newer commits to the new branch
#    (move works parent→child direction, so we need a different approach)
```

This pattern doesn't work directly because `sdf move` only moves commits **down** (to the parent). To move commits **up** (to a child), use git directly:

```bash
# 1. Create the new branch at the current tip
sdf branch api-layer
# api-layer now has commits a1-a5 (same as feature/auth)

# 2. Reset feature/auth to drop the commits you want to move
git checkout feature/auth
git reset --hard HEAD~2  # drops a4, a5

# 3. Force-push the trimmed branch
git push --force-with-lease

# 4. Sync to update the stack state
sdf sync
```

### Pattern: split current work into parent PR

This is the primary `sdf move` use case &mdash; you've been working on a branch and realize the first few commits should be their own PR:

```bash
# Stack: main ← feature/auth [setup, schema, handlers, tests]
# You want "setup" and "schema" to be a separate PR

# Move commits to the existing parent
sdf move setup schema
# Moves "setup" and "schema" to main (or whatever the parent is)
# feature/auth now only has [handlers, tests]
```

---

## How it works internally

```
Before:
  parent [p1, p2]  ←  current [c1, c2, c3]  ←  downstream [d1]

sdf move c1 c2:

Phase 1: Cherry-pick c1, c2 onto parent
  parent [p1, p2, c1, c2]

Phase 2: Rebase current to strip c1, c2
  parent [p1, p2, c1, c2]  ←  current [c3]

Phase 3: Cascade-rebase downstream
  parent [p1, p2, c1, c2]  ←  current [c3]  ←  downstream [d1]

Phase 4: Save stack state (updated BaseTips)
```

If conflicts occur during cherry-pick or rebase, Claude is invoked for auto-resolution. If that fails, the operation aborts cleanly and you can resolve manually.

---

## Tips

- **Move early, move often.** It's easier to move 1-2 commits than to untangle 10.
- **Commits must be contiguous.** If you need to move non-adjacent commits, use `git rebase -i` to reorder them first, then `sdf move`.
- **Push after moving.** `sdf move` updates local branches but doesn't push. Run `sdf sync` afterward to push all changes and update PR bases.
- **Check with `sdf status`** after moving to verify the stack looks correct.
